To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mammary gland development and breast cancer are driven by stem cells and progenitors that are regulated by a variety of signaling pathways.
the mammary gland has multiple stem cell populations and that these populations are differentially regulated by the tissue microenvironment.
mammary epithelial cells are organized in a hierarchy of stem cells, progenitor cells and differentiated cells that are maintained by systemic and local cues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular basis for the development and maintenance of the breast, with the goal of identifying the cellular and genetic basis for breast cancer.
the identification and characterization of the cells of mammary epithelial hierarchy, and how these cell populations contribute to the different phases of mammary development.
understanding how mammary epithelial stem cells, progenitor and differentiated cells interact and communicate during mammary gland development and tumorigenic transformation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mammary gland is an extremely dynamic tissue that undergoes constant remodeling and that the mammary stem cell is at the center of this remodeling.
the mammary gland stem cell hierarchy is a looking glass into the heterogeneous breast cancer landscapes.
we are far from understanding the mammary stem cell and progenitor hierarchy and its contribution to breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a new population of stem cells in the mammary gland that we call the mammary luminal progenitor cell (MLP).

we have shown that a subset of the mammary stem cells is responsible for the initiation and maintenance of breast tumors and that this subset can be defined by the expression of a unique combination of surface and secreted proteins.
we are trying to better understand the mammary stem cell compartment and the role that it plays during normal mammary development as well as breast tumorigenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mammary gland, as a model of tissue development and cancer, is a powerful system to study stem cells and their role in tissue homeostasis and disease.
the mammary gland is an excellent model system to study stem cell dynamics in a complex tissue.
the mammary stem cell and its progeny represent a dynamic system that is responsive to both local and systemic cues.
